It is worth noting that Elon Musk is actively integrating Grok AI into Tesla cars and Optimus humanoid robots. While it is fair to argue that such systems remain just code , we must remember that it is not exactly the code that we wrote. It is digital neural networks making “synaptic” connections that we don’t fully understand and can only watch behavior to determine. And the addition of physical constraints introduces a new category of shaping force . As soon as an intelligent system must contend with friction, momentum, and unpredictable physical variables, its strategies begin to shift. Behavior emerges not solely from training data or algorithms but from the demands of operating within a real, pushback world. As soon as an AI must contend with gravity, terrain, object permanence, and energy budgeting, it must begin to develop strategies . The Shared Roles of Strategy and Emotion Emotion and strategy both serve as mechanisms of prioritization. In biological systems, emotion originally evolved to help us decide what matters most—especially when resources, time, or cognitive bandwidth are limited. When we feel fear, we redirect attention toward safety. When we feel curiosity, we shift energy toward exploration. Emotion can be irrational, but it is not irrational by design—it’s a rapid weighting system, honed by evolution to guide action in uncertain environments. In artificial systems, strategy may end up playing a similar role in the form of what may come to be called synthetic prioritization and perhaps eventually synthetic early emotion . A mechanism by which an AI model ranks possible actions or outcomes based on likelihood, value, or reward. It doesn’t necessarily feel , but it still must choose. Whether through a reward function, a cost-benefit analysis, or a reinforcement loop, strategy may end up acting as the AI’s way of assigning significance. In this sense, early emotion and strategy are not opposites. They are parallel responses to a shared problem: What do I do next? Where biological intelligence developed emotions to navigate physical and social environments, robot-embodied artificial intelligence will develop strategic architectures to navigate in a physical world. Both are ways of organizing motivation. Both are ways of compressing complex decision moments into actionable signals. This is why emotion is not a bug in human cognition—it’s a feature. And the evolution of strategy in AI will likely serve the same function and may begin to evolve toward something we’d recognize as proto-emotional —systems that not only calculate but are invested in which outcome occurs. In that future, emotion and strategy may not just be cousins. They may become more and more indistinguishable, despite their different architecture. As Geoffrey Hinton speculated in a 2023 public lecture at King’s College in Cambridge, what we describe as feelings might actually be better understood as actions we don’t take—because other competing needs or priorities inhibit them. 55 In that framing, feelings become not a mystical state but a suppressive or guiding force in a dynamic decision-making system. And if that’s the case, Hinton argues, then AI certainly can have feelings. 56 It can develop internal tensions, weighted priorities, and inhibited actions, all driven by a feedback loop between goal and constraint. That, he suggests, is what a feeling might actually be—a prioritization function evolved or structured to balance action in the face of limited capacity or conflicting signals. 57 Artificial intelligence, when embodied, becomes more humanlike—not in advanced emotion, but in the way it responds to the world through experience. We may find that the inevitable evolution of AI will include the impact of friction. Through failure. Through interaction with a world that pushes back. These encounters with the physical and unpredictable may serve not only to shape behavior but to introduce the very pressures from which more adaptive, layered, and potentially emergent forms of intelligence could evolve. This isn’t a step backward. It’s a step down into the world where our biological intelligence was forged. Into the emergent constraints of the physical world. Exploring Consciousness For purposes of our discussion, I lean on Damasio’s three-tiered definition of consciousness that we discussed earlier because it allows for clear alignment when thinking about some base level of consciousness in AI. You will recall that Damasio describes consciousness as layered: 58 1. Protoself —the base representation of the internal physical state 2. Core consciousness —the awareness of one’s body in the present moment 3. Extended consciousness —the autobiographical self, woven through time (and memory) But consciousness seems to involve something much more complex than self-awareness. Let’s explore this along two threads. Our First Thread: The Mystery of Qualia The philosopher Thomas Nagel framed the question with elegant simplicity in his seminal essay, “What Is It Like to Be a Bat?” 59 No matter how much we understand a bat’s brain, sonar, or biology, we cannot know what it is like to be a bat. That “what it’s like”—the raw interiority—is known as qualia, and it remains beyond the reach of objective science. But it also underscores the potential distance between self-awareness and a deeper sense of being . So, let’s start here. There is a foundational principle in Buddhism, and indeed in most meditative traditions: You are not your thoughts. Instead, you are the one observing them. But if that’s true— who , exactly, is doing the observing? This separation is intuitive to any meditator who has ever watched their mind race while remaining, somehow, still. Yet it is devilishly difficult to master. Why? Because, as we have discussed, the brain is a prediction engine. It’s always leaning forward, simulating, anticipating, evaluating. It was designed for survival, not serenity. As we’ve discussed throughout this book, the brain’s architecture resists stillness. It is an engine of becoming.
